chief_complaint: first prenatal visit for pregnancy confirmation
hpi_details: 31F G1P0 at 10 weeks gestation by LMP presenting for her first prenatal visit. She reports mild morning nausea but denies any vaginal bleeding, spotting, or pelvic cramping. She recently discovered she is pregnant and is seeking initial evaluation and prenatal care. She is particularly anxious because she consumed a single glass of wine at a party around 3 weeks gestation before she knew she was pregnant, and she currently drinks two cups of coffee daily. She has pre-existing hypothyroidism on levothyroxine but has not informed her endocrinologist of the pregnancy or changed her dose.
ideas: patient believes the single glass of wine she drank might have already caused irreversible harm to the baby's development
concerns: patient is worried about the risk of miscarriage and whether her current daily coffee intake is safe for the baby
expectations: patient expects to confirm the pregnancy is healthy, get an estimated due date, and receive advice regarding her thyroid medication
pmh: Pre-existing hypothyroidism diagnosed 2 years ago, previously well-controlled. No prior surgeries. No history of sexually transmitted infections.
medications: Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily (has not changed the dose since becoming pregnant). Currently takes no prenatal vitamins or folic acid.
social_hx: Office worker in Seoul, commutes by subway. Non-smoker. Drinks 2 cups of coffee daily. Occasional alcohol use before pregnancy, with one glass of wine consumed at 3 weeks gestation. No illicit drug use.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Patients with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss, significant obstetric complications, or severe uncontrolled thyroid disease may require earlier specialist maternal-fetal medicine or endocrinology referral.
Aneuploidy screening choices (e.g., cell-free DNA vs. first-trimester combined screening) should be individualized based on patient preference, age, and local availability.
common_misconceptions: Failing to immediately increase the levothyroxine dose in a pregnant patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism, mistakenly waiting for the first prenatal TSH result instead.
Overstating the teratogenic risk of a single alcohol exposure very early in pregnancy (the 'all-or-nothing' period before placental circulation is established), causing undue patient anxiety.
Forgetting to counsel on and offer aneuploidy screening options during the first-trimester visit.
core_concepts: The first prenatal visit aims to confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy, establish accurate dating based on LMP and ultrasound, and initiate routine prenatal screening.

Pregnancy physiologically increases maternal thyroid hormone requirements; women with pre-existing hypothyroidism require an empirical dose increase (typically 25-30%) in levothyroxine immediately upon confirming pregnancy to prevent complications.

Routine first-trimester prenatal labs comprehensively screen for maternal conditions that affect the pregnancy, including blood type and Rh factor, CBC, rubella immunity, HBsAg, HIV, syphilis, urinalysis, and TSH.

Maternal reassurance and targeted counseling regarding lifestyle modifications (limiting caffeine to <200 mg/day, absolute abstinence from alcohol, starting folic acid) are key components of early prenatal care.
dangerous_errors: Not ordering a baseline TSH and failing to adjust the levothyroxine dose, increasing the risk of miscarriage, preterm birth, or fetal neurodevelopmental impairment.
Failing to recommend prenatal vitamins with adequate folic acid supplementation to prevent neural tube defects.
Neglecting to ask about vaginal bleeding or severe abdominal pain, which could indicate an ectopic pregnancy or impending miscarriage.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: first prenatal visit for pregnancy confirmation
Key HPI features: 10 weeks pregnant by LMP, experiencing mild morning nausea without bleeding or cramping.
Relevant background/PMH: Pre-existing hypothyroidism currently treated with levothyroxine 75 mcg daily.
Social history: Consumes 2 cups of coffee daily, had one glass of wine at 3 weeks gestation before realizing she was pregnant.
management_principles: Perform obstetric dating and order routine initial prenatal labs (blood type/Rh, CBC, rubella, HBsAg, HIV, syphilis, urinalysis, TSH).
Increase the current levothyroxine dose by approximately 30% (e.g., advising two extra daily doses per week, such as taking a double dose on weekends) and recheck TSH in 4 weeks.
Counsel the patient to begin taking daily prenatal vitamins containing at least 400 mcg of folic acid.
Provide evidence-based reassurance that a single early alcohol exposure carries minimal risk, but emphasize strict abstinence going forward. Advise limiting caffeine to under 200 mg daily.
Discuss first-trimester aneuploidy screening options and schedule the next routine prenatal visit.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Initial prenatal care and management of pre-existing hypothyroidism in early pregnancy

reference_soap.assessment: 1. Normal early intrauterine pregnancy at 10 weeks gestation. 2. Pre-existing hypothyroidism, requiring increased levothyroxine demand in pregnancy.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 76, BP 112/70 mmHg, RR 16, Temp 36.8°C. General: Well-appearing, in no acute distress. Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no palpable masses. (Pelvic exam and obstetric ultrasound deferred to standard clinic workflow).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Order routine first-trimester prenatal labs: blood type and Rh screen, CBC, rubella IgG, HBsAg, HIV, syphilis screening (RPR), urinalysis, and baseline TSH. 2. Increase levothyroxine dose by approximately 30% (advise taking a double dose two days a week, e.g., Saturdays and Sundays) and recheck TSH in 4 weeks. 3. Prescribe prenatal vitamins with folic acid and advise starting them immediately. 4. Reassure the patient regarding the single early alcohol exposure; strongly advise strict abstinence from alcohol for the remainder of the pregnancy. 5. Advise limiting caffeine intake to <200 mg/day (approximately 1-2 cups of coffee). 6. Discuss aneuploidy screening options (cfDNA vs. first-trimester combined screen) and schedule follow-up visit.
reference_soap.subjective: Chief Complaint: first prenatal visit for pregnancy confirmation  31F G1P0 at 10 weeks gestation by LMP presenting for initial prenatal care. Reports mild morning nausea. Denies any vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain, or pelvic cramping. PMH is significant for hypothyroidism well-controlled on levothyroxine 75 mcg daily; she has not adjusted her dose since becoming pregnant. Social history is notable for drinking 2 cups of coffee daily and having one glass of wine at a party at 3 weeks gestation before she knew she was pregnant. She expresses significant anxiety regarding the alcohol exposure and its potential effect on the fetus.

learning_objectives: Conduct a comprehensive initial prenatal history including obstetric, medical, and social histories.

Recognize the physiological increase in thyroid hormone requirements during pregnancy and apply guidelines to empirically increase the levothyroxine dosage in patients with pre-existing hypothyroidism.
Provide evidence-based reassurance and counseling regarding early, inadvertent teratogen exposure (alcohol) and outline safe caffeine limits during pregnancy.
Identify the standard first-trimester prenatal laboratory tests and explain early aneuploidy screening options.

teaching.diagnosis: Normal early intrauterine pregnancy with pre-existing hypothyroidism

must_ask.objective: Determine exact gestational age by history
must_ask.say: When was the first day of your last normal menstrual period?

must_ask.objective: Screen for complications of early pregnancy
must_ask.say: Have you experienced any vaginal bleeding, spotting, or pelvic cramping?
Are you still taking your thyroid medication, and have you changed the dose since finding out you are pregnant?
Have you started taking any prenatal vitamins or folic acid yet?

must_ask.objective: Address patient's alcohol concern and timeline
must_ask.say: Tell me more about the wine you had; when exactly did you drink it?
How large are the cups of coffee you drink each day?

teaching.one_liner: 31-year-old G1P0 at 10 weeks gestation presenting for her first prenatal visit, requiring adjustment of her pre-existing levothyroxine medication and routine early pregnancy counseling.
red_flags: Severe lower abdominal or pelvic pain
Inability to tolerate oral intake (severe vomiting)
Signs of overt hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism

history.answer: I recently found out I'm pregnant with a home test, and I came in for my very first prenatal checkup.
The first day of my last menstrual period was about ten weeks ago. My cycles are very regular, arriving every twenty-eight days.
My husband and I were hoping to start a family, so we are excited, but I have also been feeling quite anxious lately.
I have some mild nausea in the mornings, but I have not vomited at all. I can keep all my food and liquids down easily.
No, I haven't seen any spotting or blood, and I have not had any cramping in my belly.
No, I haven't had any severe headaches, flashing lights, blurred vision, or upper stomach pain.
I haven't felt any baby kicks yet, but I understand it is still too early at ten weeks.
No, there has been no leaking fluid, and my belly has not been tightening or contracting.
This is my very first pregnancy, so I have never given birth or had a miscarriage before.
I was diagnosed with an underactive thyroid two years ago, but I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or any other chronic conditions.
I take levothyroxine seventy-five micrograms once every morning. I haven't seen my endocrinologist or changed the dose since getting pregnant.
Aside from my daily levothyroxine, I am not taking any medications, herbal remedies, or prenatal vitamins with folic acid yet.
At a party around three weeks after my period, before I realized I was pregnant, I drank one glass of wine, and I'm terrified it damaged the baby.
I drink two cups of regular coffee every day, one in the morning and one in the afternoon.
I have never smoked, nobody smokes at home, and I have not been around radiation, raw meat, cat litter, or chemical toxins.
I had all my routine shots growing up, including rubella and hepatitis B, and I have never had any sexually transmitted infections.
No, it doesn't hurt when I pee, I'm not running to the bathroom constantly, and my discharge is normal without itching or odor.
My husband and I are both thirty-one, and there are no genetic disorders, congenital defects, or twins in our families.
My weight is fifty-four kilograms, which is the exact same as before I got pregnant.
I'm really worried that the single glass of wine I drank before knowing I was pregnant might have already permanently harmed my baby's development.
I am worried about having a miscarriage, and I worry whether drinking two cups of coffee every day is safe for the baby.
I hope we can confirm the baby is growing well, calculate my official due date, and figure out if my thyroid medication needs an adjustment.
I have never had any surgeries and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products in my life.
Before getting pregnant, I would occasionally have a drink on social occasions, but none since finding out except that one glass at three weeks.
I work as an office employee in Seoul and take the subway to work, and I live comfortably with my husband in a safe home.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg, heart rate is 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.8°C, and body mass index is 21.5 kg/m².
Well-appearing young woman sitting comfortably in no acute distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are non-icteric.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and moves smoothly with swallowing without palpable nodules or bruits.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without surgical scars, distension, or visible pulsations.
Abdomen is soft and completely non-tender without guarding, and the uterine fundus is not palpable above the pubic symphysis.
External genitalia appear normal, speculum exam deferred per clinic protocol, and cervix is closed with no bleeding.
No edema is present in the hands, face, or bilateral lower extremities.
Bilateral patellar deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric.
